deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. Folio 133 is the continuation of a German prose essay on the campaigns of Alexander the Great, carried over from folio 132 and continued on the next folio. Its content, in order:

1. Alexander turns back because of a revolt in Aria. The satrap of Aria rebels and is brought back to obedience.
2. Alexander advances again into Sogdiana in the east. Bessus, the regicide satrap of Bactria, is handed over to him as a prisoner and executed.
3. He moves against the Scythians, defeats them and reaches the Jaxartes, where he founds a border fortress (Alexandria Eschate).
4. By '328' the whole Persian Empire is said to be conquered.
5. He then plans to conquer India, described as already highly cultivated (the date 328 is repeated) and divided into monarchical and republican states.
6. He crosses the Paropamisus (Hindu Kush) into northern India as far as the Indus.
7. A last, partly illegible sentence concerns the region of Taxila.

At the lower right is a signature or annotation, apparently 'Aufs. Bauer' (perhaps 'Aufsatz'/'Aufsicht' plus a name), with a flourished 'B' beneath it.

The hand, a fairly unpracticed German Kurrent, and the school-essay character suggest a pupil's exercise or lecture notes. It is probably not Gauss's own writing, though I cannot confirm that from this page alone. It may be material that ended up among his papers, for example a family member's schoolwork. Nothing here relates to Lagrange or to any mathematics despite the bundle name.
errors: Historical dating is loose. Bessus was executed in 329 BC. The Jaxartes campaign and the founding of Alexandria Eschate also fall in 329 BC. Sogdiana was only finally pacified in 328/327 BC.
The Indian campaign began in late 327 BC, not 328 BC. The crossing of the Indus and the battle at the Hydaspes were in 326 BC. The next page's 'Frühjahr 328' should be 326.
Calling the Persian Empire wholly conquered by 328 BC is a simplification, though roughly defensible.

results.what: Narrative history of Alexander's eastern campaigns: Aria, Sogdiana, the execution of Bessus, the Jaxartes, and the advance to the Indus.
results.modern_name: Not mathematics; standard schoolbook ancient history
results.usually_credited_to: Arrian, Curtius Rufus (ancient sources); routine textbook material

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a non-mathematical history essay, probably in a pupil's hand rather than Gauss's, containing only routine textbook narrative with no mathematical content.

checkable.asserts: Trivial date arithmetic: Bessus' execution (329 BC) precedes the start of the Indian campaign (327 BC) by two years. There is nothing mathematical on the page to verify.

transcription_corrections: Line 5, word 'Scythen': the 'h' appears to have been inserted as a later correction ('Scyten' corrected to 'Scythen').

Last line: the machine reading 'In der Gegend von Taxila[?] erhielt[?] er[?] ...' is uncertain. The image appears to read roughly 'In der Gegend von Taxila stiftete er daselbst ...'; this remains tentative.
Signature: it reads 'Aufs. Bauer', possibly 'Bauerm…' or 'Bauern' as the word runs off the edge. A flourished 'B' sits below it.
Line 'Indien zu erobern welches schon sehr kultivirt war 328.' is confirmed. The '328' is repeated at the line end, apparently a marginal date.
'Satrap von Aria' is confirmed (not 'Arien' as on the previous page).
